title: Reading RISC-V instruction formats
objective: By the end of this lesson you can identify which format an instruction uses from its opcode, explain why the branch and store formats scatter their immediates, and read any base instruction without a reference card.

blocks.text: The previous lesson used two formats. There are six in the base set, and they exist because different instructions need different things: some need two source registers, some need a constant, some need a large constant, and some need a jump target. Each format spends the same 32 bits differently.
The six, and what each is for

rows: Register arithmetic: add, sub, and, xor
rd — a store produces no result
rd — a branch produces no result

blocks.title: The missing field tells you what the instruction does
blocks.text: S and B have no destination register because neither produces a value: a store writes to memory, a branch changes where execution goes. Their five bits of rd space were reclaimed for the immediate. Reading a format's field list therefore tells you the shape of the operation before you know which instruction it is.

blocks.caption: An S-type immediate, split across two places
lines: | imm[11:5]  |  rs2   |  rs1   |funct3| imm[4:0]|  opcode  |
/* Compare with I-type, where the same 12 bits sit contiguously at
31:20. They were split here so that rs1, rs2 and funct3 stay in
exactly the positions they occupy in R-type and I-type. */

blocks.text: The reason is the one the previous lesson gave: fixed register positions let the hardware start reading the register file immediately, before it knows what the instruction is. Reassembling a split immediate is free — it is wiring, with no logic in between. A misaligned register field would cost a selector on the path that matters most.

blocks.title: The bit-13 trick in the branch format
blocks.text: A B-type immediate encodes a 13-bit signed offset in 12 bits, by leaving out the lowest bit and defining it as always zero. That is legitimate because every instruction is 4-byte aligned, so no branch target can ever be at an odd address. One bit saved by encoding a fact the architecture already guarantees — the same kind of reasoning as the dedicated zero register.
Identifying a format from the opcode

blocks.caption: The opcodes you will meet most
lines: 0110011   R    register arithmetic          add, sub, and, or, xor, sll
0010011   I    immediate arithmetic         addi, andi, ori, slli
0000011   I    loads                        lb, lh, lw, ld
0100011   S    stores                       sb, sh, sw, sd
1100011   B    branches                     beq, bne, blt, bge
1101111   J    jump and link                jal
1100111   I    jump and link register       jalr
0110111   U    load upper immediate         lui
/* Read the low 7 bits first, and you know the layout of the other 25. */

blocks.text: Reading one you have never seen

blocks.caption: Decoding 0x00a58533 step by step
lines: opcode = 0110011  -> R-type, register arithmetic
funct3 = 000
funct7 = 0000000  -> add, not sub
therefore: add x10, x11, x10
/* Seven bits told you the layout; the rest is reading fields off it. */

blocks.text: How many instructions the base set has

The 64-bit base integer set is small enough to list on one page. Everything else — multiplication, atomics, floating point, compressed encodings, vectors — is an optional extension named by a letter, and a given chip states which it implements. That modularity is the design decision that distinguishes RISC-V from architectures where every feature is mandatory forever.

blocks.title: Decode without a reference
steps: Write a decoder that reads the low 7 bits, selects the layout, and prints the fields
Feed it 0x00a58533 and confirm you get add x10, x11, x10
Feed it 0x02a30293 from the previous lesson and confirm addi x5, x6, 42
Encode sw x5, 8(x6) by hand as an S-type and check the immediate split is right
Encode beq x5, x6, +16 as a B-type and confirm the lowest bit is not stored
Explain why a branch to an odd address cannot be encoded, and why that is not a limitation
Take any four-byte word from a real binary and decode it with your program
Compare your answer with objdump on the same address
blocks.expected: A decoder of your own that agrees with objdump, and two hand encodings whose scattered immediates you got right. The B-type exercise is the one worth doing carefully — understanding why the lowest bit is free is what makes the rest of the encoding feel designed rather than arbitrary.

cheatsheet: Six base formats: R, I, S, B, U, J — each spends 32 bits differently
R: two sources, no constant · I: one source and a 12-bit constant
S and B have no destination register, because a store and a branch produce no value
U and J carry large constants and have no source register
Immediates are split so rs1, rs2 and funct3 stay at fixed positions
Reassembling a split immediate is wiring; a moved register field would cost a selector
B-type encodes 13 bits in 12 by omitting the lowest, which is always zero
Read the low 7 bits first and the layout of the other 25 is determined
The base integer set fits on a page; everything else is an optional lettered extension

checkpoint.prompt: Why does the S-type format have no rd field?
checkpoint.explanation: Those five bits were reclaimed for the immediate. The same reasoning applies to B-type: a branch produces no value either. Reading which field a format lacks tells you the shape of the operation.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is the S-type immediate split across bits 31:25 and 11:7 instead of being contiguous?

choices.B: Because 12 contiguous bits were not available
choices.C: So rs1, rs2 and funct3 stay at the same bit positions as in other formats, letting the register file be read before decoding finishes
choices.D: To make decoding harder to reverse-engineer

checkpoint.explanation: Reassembling the immediate is pure wiring with no logic. Moving a register field would put a selector on the critical path, which is far more expensive.

checkpoint.prompt: How does a B-type instruction encode a 13-bit offset in 12 bits?

choices.B: It omits the lowest bit and defines it as zero
choices.D: It stores the offset divided by 4 with rounding

checkpoint.explanation: Is safe because instructions are 4-byte aligned. The architecture already guarantees that no instruction sits at an odd address, so that bit carries no information. Encoding a fact the architecture guarantees buys a bit of range for free.

checkpoint.prompt: You have an unknown 32-bit word. What do you read first?

choices.C: It must be looked up in a table of all possible instructions
choices.D: The low 7 bits — the opcode sets the layout of the rest

checkpoint.explanation: That is why the opcode sits at the bottom. Once you know the format, every other field's position is fixed and decoding is mechanical.
